claims.text: Pronounced atomic size mismatches in high-entropy nanoalloys induce lattice distortions.
Lattice distortions suppress atomic diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Suppressed atomic diffusion chemically and structurally stabilizes high-entropy nanoalloys against high-temperature degradation.
The proposed initial materials are equiatomic, nanoscale, single-phase solid solutions.
Atomic size mismatch can be varied through compositional tuning while retaining a suitable high-entropy nanoalloy comparison.
Lattice distortions resulting from atomic size mismatch are the structural mediator of stability.
Lattice distortions hinder atomic diffusion pathways by impeding thermally activated atomic migration.
Hindering thermally activated atomic migration reduces phase separation.
Hindering thermally activated atomic migration reduces coarsening and helps preserve a single-phase structure.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will exhibit lower rates of phase separation than alloys with minimized mismatch.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, alloys with greater atomic size mismatch will exhibit lower rates of coarsening than alloys with minimized mismatch.
A nanoalloy with minimized atomic size mismatch is predicted to undergo enhanced diffusion-driven phase separation.
A nanoalloy with minimized atomic size mismatch is predicted to undergo enhanced grain growth.
The prediction is bounded to equiatomic nanoscale high-entropy alloys undergoing thermal aging where oxidation and other extrinsic degradation mechanisms are not dominant.
Chemical ordering may be an alternative stabilization factor whose contribution relative to lattice distortion remains uncertain.
Failure of the high-mismatch group to show significantly lower phase-separation and coarsening rates than the minimized-mismatch group would falsify the proposed governing role of lattice distortion.
